newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's new defence chief takes aim at N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's new defence chief takes aim at N.Korea.

text.p: South Korea's new defence minister delivered a swift verbal attack on North Korea after taking office on Friday, blaming Pyongyang for escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula.
In his inauguration speech, Kim Dong-jin also pledged to lead a military force strong enough to "win every war".

He took aim at North Korea, which has recently drawn condemnation from Seoul, the United Nations and the European Union following an incursion of one of its submarines which delivered 26 agents into the south last month.
Twenty-two of the 26 infiltrators have been killed by South Korean troops or found dead. One was captured alive and a hunt is on for the remaining three.
"North Korea, amid continued instability in its system and by retaining its strategies toward the South, is heightening tension on the Korean peninsula," Kim said.
Kim replaced Lee Yang-ho as chairman of the joint chiefs of staff and defence minister in a sweeping reshuffle on Thursday of Seoul's top military brass.
The shakeup followed fierce criticism of the military over the ease with which the north's Shark-class submarine penetrated South Korean coastal defences without triggering any alarm.
Analysts said Kim's appointment also reflected President Kim Young-sam's desire to tighten South Korean defences against any possible future northern provocation.

National security remains tight as South Korean troops continue a massive manhunt for the fugitive northern agents, who have been blamed by Seoul for the murder of three villagers in the east coast area of Mount Odae in early October.

Adding to the atmosphere of heightened security, the Capital Defence Command said on Friday it would conduct an anti-espionage exercise in Seoul and surrounding areas between October 21 and November 9.
A Command spokesman said soldiers from army units stationed in Seoul, along with policemen and reserve forces, would participate in the drill.
"It's a sort of routine drill for the capital defence units and there will be no massive movement of soldiers or equipment as we see in nationwide drills," the spokesman said.
South and North Korea have been technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean War ended in a truce, rather than a peace pact.
